sections.title: Quick Answer
sections.content: **Hallow vs Abide** comes down to tradition and depth: Hallow is the bigger, Catholic-rooted library — rosaries, novenas, hundreds of guided sessions — while Abide is lighter and broadly evangelical, built around short daily meditations and one of the deepest sleep-story catalogs in the category. Neither one puts Scripture on the screen you actually check without opening anything — that's the free layer **FaithWall** adds underneath whichever one you pick.

**FaithWall** is our app, so weigh that against everything below — here's the honest case anyway. It doesn't compete with Hallow or Abide's guided sessions; it does the one thing neither app does, which is put today's verse on your lock screen automatically, no session required.

sections.text: If you're weighing **hallow vs abide**, you've probably noticed both apps do roughly the same job on paper — audio-guided prayer and meditation built around Scripture — and both have a free tier that feels thin once the novelty wears off. The real difference isn't a feature on a spec sheet. It's tradition and depth. Hallow grew up inside a Catholic framework and has become the deepest audio library in the category. Abide leans lighter and more nondenominational, and its sleep-story catalog is arguably the best reason to open it at all. Pick based on which one of those two things you actually want.
What each app is actually for

Hallow is a guided prayer and meditation app rooted in Catholic tradition — full Rosaries, novenas, the Ignatian Examen, Lectio Divina, and a rotating cast of narrators reading over ambient music. It has broadened past a strictly Catholic audience, but the structure still shows: sessions follow liturgical rhythms, saints' feast days, and sacramental language most Protestant apps skip entirely. Abide takes a different shape. It's a Bible meditation and sleep app organized by feeling, not tradition — pick anxiety, grief, gratitude, or parenting, and a narrator walks you through slow breathing paired with Scripture read in context. Abide's evangelical, nondenominational lean means less liturgical vocabulary and more of a calm, therapy-adjacent structure built around a specific mood.
Be still, and know that I am God.

Both apps run the same playbook: free daily content, a subscription for the full library. Line up the numbers and the story gets clearer:

| | Hallow | Abide |
|---|---|---|
| Free tier | Daily audio, a small slice of the full catalog | Daily meditation plus a handful of sleep stories |
| Monthly | $9.99 | $9.99 |
| Annual | $69.99 (family plan $119.99/yr, up to 6 accounts) | $39.99 |
| Lifetime | $149.99 one-time | ~$149.99 one-time |
| Sleep content | Rosary and Compline audio, a moderate catalog | 365+ dedicated sleep stories — the deeper catalog |

Abide's annual price undercuts Hallow's by roughly $30, and its sleep-story library is the larger of the two — if falling asleep to Scripture is the actual use case, that's the tell. Hallow's family plan is the better deal once more than two people in a household are using it, and its Catholic devotional content — full Rosaries, novenas tied to the liturgical calendar — has no real equivalent inside Abide.
The gap a guided session can't cover

Both apps solve the same problem the same way: you open them, sit through a session, close them, and the rest of the day looks the same as before. That's not a flaw — it's the format. A guided session needs your attention, so it can only happen once or twice a day. **FaithWall** covers the other twenty-three hours. Instead of a session, it puts one verse on your lock screen and rotates it through a themed pack — Anxiety, Strength, Gratitude, Grief — so Scripture shows up every time you glance at your phone, not just during the ten minutes you set aside for Hallow or Abide.

sections.text: The common mistake is trying to make a session app cover the whole day. You finish a Hallow Rosary or an Abide sleep story, screenshot a verse that landed, and set it as your wallpaper by hand. It holds for about a week. The image wasn't designed for the lock-screen surface — the crop is off, the text sits wrong — and by day ten you're back to a photo of your dog. A guided-prayer app was never built to live on your lock screen, and neither was a screenshot. That's the exact gap **FaithWall** closes: no screenshotting, no manual swap, just a themed pack that installs itself through iOS Focus modes and keeps rotating.

sections.content: If you're still deciding between the two, start with whichever free tier you actually finish a full week using — then add the free lock-screen layer underneath it. It doesn't compete with either app's session; it just fills the hours neither one is designed to reach.

sections.text: For most people asking **hallow vs abide**, the honest split is tradition first, then budget. If you're Catholic or drawn to liturgical structure — the Rosary, novenas, saints' feast days — Hallow's depth is hard to match. If you want something lighter, cheaper, and built around sleep and specific moods rather than a devotional calendar, Abide wins on both price and its sleep-story catalog. Either way, add it for free — it's the piece that keeps working after the session ends. For a fuller Hallow breakdown, including denominational lean and iOS integration, see [how the two pair up specifically](/faithwall-vs-hallow).

sections.content: Hallow and Abide aren't really competing with each other for the same hour of your day — they're competing on which tradition and which mood-first structure fits you. Whichever you choose, it's still a session you have to remember to open. The lock screen is the one surface that doesn't ask you to remember anything.
